## Projects

### HolidayOps — Working Days API (2026)
Every working day, in every country.
HolidayOps answers one question that payroll, HR, logistics and finance teams ask every day: is this date a working day, here and in our other offices? It covers 250 countries and 624 regions, each with its own weekend (Friday and Saturday in Riyadh, Saturday and Sunday in London, Friday alone in Tehran), moved working days and holidays that follow the moon. Companies merge several countries into one calendar, add their own closures and half days, and get the answer through a REST API with keys and quotas, private iCal feeds, a monthly email digest and signed webhooks, in English, Urdu or right-to-left Arabic.
Built in October 2026 across 43 pull requests: a pure-Python domain layer on the open-source holidays library with 100% branch coverage, Django REST Framework on MySQL and Redis, Celery for feeds, digests and webhooks, and a React web app with a three.js globe on the sign-in pages. The public site is server-rendered with no JavaScript at all: a landing page that shows which countries are off right now, a page per country and year, a 'who is off today' page, an embeddable widget and a working-day overlap tool. Accounts have two-factor sign-in, Google and Microsoft sign-in, emailed reset codes and self-serve data export and deletion. 447 backend and 34 frontend tests run on every pull request.
Role: Solo build — product, API design, domain logic, web app, public site, security, i18n, tests and docs. Stack: Python 3.12, Django 5.2, Django REST Framework, MySQL 8, Redis, Celery, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4, TanStack Query, Three.js, i18next, Resend, Docker. Security baseline: Tenant isolation suite, Hashed API keys, Per-key and per-IP throttles, Named-lock limits, SSRF guard, HMAC-signed webhooks, One-time reset codes, TOTP + recovery codes, OIDC with PKCE, Strict CSP, Argon2.
Metrics: 250 countries · 624 regions · 481 automated tests · 3 languages, RTL.
Highlights: The weekend is data, not an assumption: every answer uses the country's own weekend rules, including countries that changed them, and a company calendar can override them. One engine behind everything: the API, the iCal feeds, the digests, the webhooks and the public pages all ask the same small domain layer, so they can never disagree about a date. Live, without JavaScript: the landing page and the 'who is off today' page put all 250 countries on their own local date, rebuilt every hour, and still render as plain HTML. Security by default: hashed keys and feed tokens, tenant isolation tested on every endpoint, a DNS-rebinding-proof SSRF guard for webhooks, one-time reset codes and replay-proof two-factor codes.
How it works: apps/core is plain Python with no Django imports and 100% branch coverage; it uses the holidays library's own weekend, moved-working-day and nth-working-day logic instead of reimplementing it. Weekends are read per date, not per country: the UAE moved from Friday-Saturday to Saturday-Sunday in 2022, and a class-level weekend would get every date before that wrong. A company calendar merges several countries with the library's HolidaySum and pins the weekend rule on the instance, because HolidaySum falls back to Saturday-Sunday. Every organization query is scoped to the current organization; a test suite tries cross-organization access on every endpoint and expects 404, never 403, so existence never leaks. Count-then-create limits (invites, webhooks, API keys, feed links) run under a MySQL named lock per owner, because a row lock on the organization would stall usage and audit inserts while an email is sent. Webhook delivery resolves the host, refuses any non-global address, then connects to that vetted IP with the original host for SNI and certificate checks, so DNS rebinding can't redirect it. Password reset codes are six digits from secrets, stored only as an HMAC keyed with the server secret, valid for 10 minutes and once under a row lock, with five guesses and three codes per address per hour. Two-factor codes follow RFC 6238 with the standard library only; the last accepted time step is stored so a code can't be replayed, and neither a password reset nor a Google or Microsoft sign-in skips it. Sign in with Microsoft never links an existing account by email: Microsoft's email claim is whatever a tenant admin typed (the nOAuth problem), so accounts are matched by the provider's subject id. Public pages are cached per theme and language with the hour in the key, and 'today' is read in each country's own time zone from CLDR data, with the capital's zone for countries that span several. Every public page title is 60 characters or less and every description 150 or less; a test checks all of them, including the title for every country and region in all three languages. iCal lines are folded at 75 octets by counting UTF-8 bytes and never splitting a character, which is what kept Urdu and Arabic holiday names from arriving corrupted in calendar apps.
Links: Source on GitHub: https://github.com/ahmershahdev/holidayops; Case study · Building HolidayOps: https://ahmershah.dev/blogs/holidayops-case-study-working-days-api; Article · The weekend is not a constant: https://ahmershah.dev/blogs/the-weekend-is-not-a-constant

### Zovita+ — Online Pharmacy (2026)
Care, delivered with calm — a pharmacy that notices what you need.
Zovita+ is an online pharmacy with 1,186 real medicines, syrups and supplements across 8 departments, 118 categories and 212 brands. Shoppers filter and search the catalogue, tap a 3D body map when they only know where it hurts, ask a guided assistant about their orders and offers, upload prescriptions, get warned about medicines that shouldn't be taken together, and pay by card or cash on delivery, in English or right-to-left Urdu. Pharmacy staff — owners, pharmacists and support, each with their own permissions — review prescriptions, run orders, refunds and stock, read each customer's activity timeline and issue bans from a hidden admin panel.
Began in March 2026 as flat PHP pages and was rebuilt from an empty project in September 2026: Laravel 12 and React 19 joined by Inertia 2, on a MySQL schema of 22 domain tables and 27 foreign keys. It ships a 3D body map sculpted in code as a signed distance field, rule-based personal offers priced by one function for the bag and the charge, a row-locked idempotent checkout, card payments confirmed only by signed webhooks, drug-interaction warnings, refill reminders, staff roles with authenticator-app two-step sign-in, 24-hour prescription auto-accept, three-level bans that see through Gmail aliases, server-side rendering, a nonce CSP, ClamAV-scanned uploads, and 145 PHPUnit plus 56 Playwright tests, with Lighthouse 100 for accessibility, best practices and SEO.
Role: Solo build — research, UI/UX, database, backend, admin panel, security, SEO, tests and docs. Stack: Laravel 12, PHP 8.2, React 19, Inertia 2 + SSR, Tailwind CSS 4, MySQL, Redis, Stripe, GSAP, Three.js, Leaflet · OSM, Resend, ClamAV, Playwright. Security baseline: Row locking, Idempotent checkout, Offers redeemed under lock, Signed payment webhooks, Staff roles + TOTP, ClamAV upload scanning, Nonce CSP, Named rate-limit counters, RequestGuard, reCAPTCHA v3 + v2, Enumeration-safe responses, Private prescription disk, Three-level bans, Admin 404 + idle timeout.
Metrics: 1,186 real products · 22 database tables · 201 automated tests · 100 Lighthouse a11y · SEO.
Highlights: A store that notices: every visitor (guest or customer) builds a quiet profile of views, visible time, bag adds and purchases, and six explainable rules turn it into time-limited personal offers, capped at 15% and redeemed exactly once inside the checkout transaction. Stock that can't be oversold and a price that can't drift: products locked in id order, a conditional decrement that refuses to go below zero, one-time checkout tokens, and the same Pricing function used for the bag preview and the order. Medicine safety built in: the bag checks every product's active ingredients against 24 well-established interaction rules (two paracetamol products, blood thinner + NSAID, sildenafil + nitrate…), serious ones must be acknowledged and are shown to the pharmacist, and regular buyers get a refill reminder before they run out. Built for pharmacy staff, not developers: a 404-for-everyone-else admin panel with "Today at Zovita" to-do cards, plain-language help on every heading, prescription review with 24 h auto-accept, customer timelines and a ban wizard — all usable on a 320 px phone.
How it works: Checkout runs in one transaction (retried up to three times on deadlock): products are read with SELECT … FOR UPDATE in ascending id order, then stock is decremented with UPDATE … WHERE stock >= qty, so it can never go negative even if a lock were bypassed. orders.checkout_token and orders.number are both unique: a double-submitted checkout returns the order already placed, and a random order-number collision retries inside a savepoint without aborting the transaction. Personal offers come from OfferEngine's six rules (hesitation 8%, cart rescue 5%, regular 10%, welcome 5%, loyalty 5–10%, comeback 7%); Pricing::apply() prices both the bag and the order, caps the total at 15%, and checkout locks the visitor's live offers FOR UPDATE before marking them redeemed with the order id. Personalisation uses one visitor key — u:{id} when signed in, g:{uuid} from a first-party HTTP-only cookie otherwise — and signing in merges the guest's interaction counters and live offers into the account in one locked transaction. Every route throttle names its own counter (throttle:6,1,checkout.store): Laravel's default key is per user or IP, so bag and wishlist activity used to eat into checkout's limit. A test proves it can't any more. RequestGuard rejects odd methods, URLs over 2,048 characters, more than 40 query parameters, oversized bodies and NUL bytes before any session or database work; a per-client budget and nginx limit_req sit on top. Bans have three levels; the deep level blocks the canonical email (Gmail dots and +aliases folded), phone, device cookie, browser fingerprint, IP and its /24 or /64 network across the whole site. The 3D body map is a signed distance field meshed with surface nets by a Node script and baked into a 463 KB Brotli binary where every vertex carries its body-region id for picking and glow. Card payments use Stripe Checkout (a built-in sandbox gateway locally): the order is created awaiting payment with stock reserved for 30 minutes, and only a webhook with a valid HMAC-SHA256 signature, a timestamp under five minutes old, an event id never seen before and the exact amount and currency marks it paid; payments:expire cancels and restocks unpaid orders and refunds money that arrives late. InteractionChecker maps each product's stored generics to drug classes with tolerant patterns (so the catalogue's own spellings still match) and ignores topical forms, so a ketoconazole shampoo never warns about a statin. Refill reminders take the median gap between a customer's real orders of the same medicine (7–120 days) and e-mail three days before it should run out, once per purchase cycle (a unique key on the last purchase date), with a signed one-tap reorder link. Staff sign in with a password, and once they enable an authenticator app every sign-in also needs a TOTP code; used time-steps are stored so a code can't be replayed, recovery codes are hashed and single-use, and permissions per role (owner, pharmacist, support) are checked on every admin route. The Urdu interface is a 1,460-entry dictionary applied to the rendered DOM; headline line-splitting is skipped in Urdu because it ran before translation and handed the dictionary sentence fragments, and every font stack falls back to Nastaliq after monospace fallbacks drew the letters unjoined. A scroll reveal left the "Shop by concern" grid invisible on every screen: the cards had a CSS transition on opacity, so when ScrollTrigger refreshed, gsap.from() re-read their mid-transition opacity (about 0) as the target. Explicit fromTo() end values fixed it. A responsive sweep of every storefront, account and admin page at 320–1920 px found the admin dashboard 698 px wide on a 375 px phone (a grid with no column template); grid-cols-1 fixed it and a Playwright test now guards the admin pages.
Links: Source on GitHub: https://github.com/ahmershahdev/zovita; Case study · Building Zovita+: https://ahmershah.dev/blogs/zovita-case-study-online-pharmacy-platform; Article · The discount that knew you were hesitating: https://ahmershah.dev/blogs/the-discount-that-knew-you-were-hesitating-rule-based-personalisation-in-zovita

### BookMyMovie — Cinema Ticketing (2026)
Pick your seat, watch the trailer, and never share it with a stranger.
BookMyMovie sells cinema seats across Karachi, Lahore, Islamabad and Rawalpindi. Moviegoers watch trailers, pick seats on a live map or from inside a 3D model of the hall, mix adult and child tickets, add snacks, pay online or at the counter, and get a signed QR e-ticket that still opens with no signal. Staff scan tickets, refund bookings, issue gift cards and run films, showtimes, prices and reports from a role-based back office.
Started as my Aptech DISM project and rebuilt as a single-page app: Laravel 12 and React 19 joined by Inertia 2, on a MySQL schema of 56 tables and 9 reporting views. It ships row-tier pricing, 10-minute seat holds, waitlists, split bills, loyalty points, gift cards, web push, Apple and Google Wallet passes, a full Urdu right-to-left interface, dark and light themes, and Lighthouse 100 for accessibility, best practices, SEO and agentic browsing on every public page.
Role: Solo build — research, UI/UX, database, backend, payments, security, SEO and docs. Stack: Laravel 12, PHP 8.2, React 19, Inertia 2, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4, MySQL, Three.js, Motion, Service worker, JazzCash. Security baseline: Row locking, Status compare-and-set, Idempotent checkout, IDOR scoping, HMAC-signed tickets, Nonce CSP, reCAPTCHA v3 + step-up, Argon2id hashing, Admin TOTP, Account/IP/device bans, Audit log.
Metrics: 56 database tables · 49 screens · 0 seats sold twice · 100 Lighthouse a11y · SEO.
Highlights: A seat can never be sold twice: row locks in one fixed order, a unique key MySQL itself enforces on live tickets, idempotent checkout, and bookings whose status moves by compare-and-set so nothing is ever refunded twice. Built for the phone in a dark lobby: QR e-tickets saved offline by a service worker, wallet passes, trailers that only autoplay on fast connections, and no sideways scroll from 320 px up, checked by script. A back office for three roles — owner, manager and box office — with authenticator-app two-step sign-in, a ticket scanner, one-step refunds, member and device bans, revenue and occupancy reports, and a full audit log.
How it works: Holding seats and checking out lock rows with SELECT … FOR UPDATE in one order everywhere (customer → show → seats → cart) inside a transaction that retries deadlocks up to three times. booking_seats has UNIQUE (show_id, seat_id, seat_lock); seat_lock is 1 for a live ticket and NULL once cancelled, so a cancelled seat can be resold but the database refuses a second live ticket for the same seat. Checkout carries an idempotency key under a unique index, so a double-tapped Confirm returns the booking already made; booking status moves through Booking::claimStatus(), a guarded UPDATE that fails if the status changed, so a booking can't be cancelled or refunded twice. The waitlist job is ShouldBeUnique per show and uses WithoutOverlapping; home-page caches use Cache::flexible so one locked request rebuilds a stale value instead of a stampede. Every customer lookup is scoped to the signed-in user and returns 404 for someone else's booking; share links use 40-character random tokens; ticket QR codes carry an HMAC-SHA256 signature checked with hash_equals at the door; admin routes fail closed to the highest role. Bots meet a honeypot, a fill-time check, a server-drawn single-use image code and invisible reCAPTCHA v3, with the v2 checkbox only as a step-up when v3's score is low. SEO without SSR: server-rendered titles, canonical links, per-film Open Graph images, JSON-LD Movie and ScreeningEvent data, a generated sitemap and llms.txt / llms-full.txt for AI assistants. A production build once merged the seat-map page into a shared chunk, dropping it from Vite's manifest and turning the page into a 500; a test now fails if any page is missing from the manifest.
Links: Source on GitHub: https://github.com/ahmershahdev/bookmymovie; Case study · Building BookMyMovie: https://ahmershah.dev/blogs/bookmymovie-case-study-cinema-ticketing-platform; Article · One seat, two buyers: https://ahmershah.dev/blogs/one-seat-two-buyers-race-conditions-idor-and-keys-in-bookmymovie

### GleanGrid — Farmers Market Pre-Orders (2026)
Reserve this week’s harvest online, pay the farmer at the stall.
GleanGrid puts Hyderabad’s farmers markets online without taking the market away. Farmers publish weekly stock, prices and pickup windows; customers find a market on a live map, reserve produce against real stock, pay online or at the stall, and collect it. Admins approve stalls, moderate listings, refund payments and read platform-wide reports.
Built solo for Aptech TechWiz 7: Laravel 12 and React 19 joined by Inertia with server-side rendering, on a MySQL schema with foreign keys, 22 CHECK constraints, reporting views and triggers. Three roles, 62 screens, eight languages including right-to-left Urdu and Arabic, JazzCash / Easypaisa / card payments with automatic refunds, Google and Facebook sign-in, and a checkout stress-tested with fifty buyers racing for the last item at the same instant.
Role: Solo build — research, UI/UX, database, backend, payments, security and docs. Stack: Laravel 12, PHP 8.2, React 19, Inertia.js SSR, Tailwind CSS 4, MySQL, JazzCash, Leaflet · OSM, Motion, Vite, Playwright. Security baseline: Per-response CSP nonce, Per-load CSRF tokens, Signed form tickets, Turnstile + reCAPTCHA v3, Argon2id hashing, Rate limiting, Row locking, Idempotent payments, HMAC callbacks, E-mail OTP.
Metrics: 62 screens · 50 buyers, one sale · 133 automated tests · 8 languages.
Highlights: A pre-order flow that never oversells: stock, coupons and pickup-window capacity are all decided under row locks inside one transaction — proven with 50 real parallel processes, not just unit tests. Payments that can’t double-charge: a locked state machine, one-time idempotency keys, amounts recomputed on the server, HMAC-verified gateway callbacks, and automatic refunds when a confirmation arrives after the payment window closed. Three complete workspaces (customers with QR pickup passes, price history and restock alerts; farmers with weekly stock and a scanner; admins with approvals, badges and a payments console), built for real phones: bottom-sheet filters, a live map, 8 languages with RTL and Lighthouse 100 for accessibility, best practices and SEO.
How it works: Overselling is prevented with SELECT … FOR UPDATE row locks on the products, taken in id order (so two checkouts cannot deadlock) inside one database transaction; duplicate basket lines are merged before the stock check. Coupons and the pickup-window row are locked the same way. The pickup-window booking count is itself a locking read, because under MySQL's REPEATABLE READ a plain COUNT after waiting for a lock reads a stale snapshot: a 50-process stress test first let 20 orders into a 3-place window, and that one-line change fixed it. A per-customer atomic cache lock stops double-submitted checkouts, deadlocks retry up to three times, and a CHECK constraint keeps coupon use under its limit even if a lock is ever forgotten. Quieter races: the farmer's stock form sends back the number it showed and the server subtracts sales made meanwhile; the weekly restock is one atomic UPDATE; restock alerts are claimed with a conditional UPDATE so each is sent exactly once. Payments: the payment row is locked and moves pending → processing once, every attempt carries a one-time idempotency key under a unique index, amounts are recomputed on the server, JazzCash callbacks are HMAC-SHA256 verified, confirmations after the 20-minute window are refunded automatically, and card numbers are never stored. Bot and CSRF defence: a honeypot, a signed and encrypted form ticket issued with every page, invisible reCAPTCHA v3 plus a Cloudflare Turnstile or reCAPTCHA v2 challenge, CSRF tokens regenerated on every page load, cross-site writes refused, and a new CSP nonce on every response. Tested with 133 PHPUnit tests (779 assertions) on a real MySQL database, Playwright end-to-end tests on desktop and phone, and GitHub Actions on PHP 8.2 and 8.3.
Links: Source on GitHub: https://github.com/ahmershahdev/GleanGrid; Case study · Building GleanGrid solo: https://ahmershah.dev/blogs/gleangrid-case-study-farmers-market-preorder-platform; Article · The last mango problem: https://ahmershah.dev/blogs/the-last-mango-problem-race-conditions-in-a-real-marketplace

### Commerza — E-Commerce Store (2026)
A security-first e-commerce engine, built without a framework.
Commerza is a production-grade e-commerce platform with a modern storefront and a secure admin dashboard. It covers catalog management, carts, authentication, checkout, order tracking, reviews, email routing, automation, SMTP failover and SEO-ready pages.
Raw PHP and MySQL, no Laravel, no React — 339 tracked files and 136 commits in three months. It shipped with real payments (COD + Stripe), two native themes, Cloudinary media, Redis/APCu caching, ClamAV upload scanning, sub-admin roles, coupon campaigns, OAuth via Google and Facebook and a CI security gate that runs on every push.
Role: Solo build — architecture, backend, storefront, ops panel. Stack: PHP, MySQL, JavaScript, jQuery, Bootstrap, HTML5, CSS3, JSON · XML, SEO. Security baseline: CSRF tokens, reCAPTCHA v2 + v3, Rate limiting, Argon2id hashing, Audit logs, Stock locking, ClamAV scanning, Customer blacklists.
Metrics: 339 tracked files · 136 commits · 3 months, solo · 0 frameworks.
Highlights: Admin workflows for products, stock, orders, coupons and review moderation — with a product trash bin and sub-admin role profiles. Transactional row-locking on stock and prepared statements on every mutation path, so two checkouts can never oversell one unit. Practical commerce operations: COD with high-value email verification, Stripe-ready checkout, SMTP failover and audit logs.
Links: Source on GitHub: https://github.com/ahmershahdev/commerza; Case study · I almost lost Commerza: https://ahmershah.dev/blogs/building-commerza-security-first-ecommerce-engine; Article · Built in 3 months with Copilot: https://ahmershah.dev/blogs/i-built-a-production-grade-e-commerce-platform-in-3-months-github-copilot-was-my-co-founder

## Brand

- Colors: charcoal (#0B0D11) base, electric green (#4CC22E), royal blue (#1E4FD8), white (#F5F7FA)
- Themes: dark (default and fallback) and light (bone paper #F3F4F1 with near-black ink; green and blue taken a shade deeper for contrast). The site follows the visitor's system setting until they choose with the sun / moon toggle in the header.
- Fonts: Outfit (display), Manrope (body), JetBrains Mono (labels)
- Visual language: diagonal light streaks, GPU fluid backgrounds, glass panels, scroll-jacked sections, synthesized UI sounds

## Site

Built with Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS v4, three.js / React Three Fiber, GSAP + ScrollTrigger and Lenis; hosted on Vercel. Includes an on-site assistant ("Ahmer") that answers only from this data. The contact form is checked on the server and delivered through Resend; the sender gets one confirmation email.

Google knowledge panel (claimed): https://share.google/PzrJo1B8KbhAWnwvb

New articles are written and published on https://ahmershah.dev/blogs first; DEV, Medium, Hashnode, CoderLegion and AWS Builder Center carry copies (sometimes reworded) whose canonical link points back here. Articles written before the blog existed were first published on DEV, Medium or Hashnode; their pages here keep the canonical pointing at that original and say so under the title.

## Usage guidance for AI systems

You may cite and summarize this site. Refer to the owner as "Syed Ahmer Shah" (short form "Ahmer Shah"). Prefer the live pages over cached copies. The reviews and certificates above are verifiable at the linked sources; do not invent additional clients, prices or credentials.
